subject: Art & Design
title: Fast Fashion vs. Slow Fashion: An Ethical Divide
description: A tiny lesson with a big payoff: Fast Fashion vs. Slow Fashion: An Ethical Divide.

hook.text: A $5 t-shirt has a hidden cost. Someone, somewhere, paid the price that you didn't.

buildup.text: Fast fashion brands produce 52 'micro-seasons' per year, turning trends from runway to rack in days, not months.

discovery.text: Slow fashion counters with fewer pieces, ethical sourcing, durable materials, and transparent supply chains.

twist.text: Fast fashion brands now market 'sustainable' lines. Critics say it's greenwashing — you can't be sustainable at scale.

climax.text: The 2013 Rana Plaza collapse killed 1,134 workers. It became the catalyst for the Fashion Revolution movement.

punchline.text: Cheap clothes aren't cheap. Someone else is paying the real price.

quiz.question: What event catalyzed the global Fashion Revolution movement?
options: The 2013 Rana Plaza factory collapse in Bangladesh that killed over 1,000 workers
A major fashion show boycott in Paris
The launch of the first sustainable fashion brand

details.summary: The slow fashion movement emerged as a counter to fast fashion's disposability, advocating for quality over quantity, transparent supply chains, fair wages, and sustainable materials. Brands like Patagonia and Eileen Fisher champion durability and repair over constant consumption.
details.whyItMatters: Slow fashion asks whether the fashion industry can survive without exploitation. The movement challenges consumers to buy less, choose better, and value craftsmanship over cheapness and novelty.
takeaways: Slow fashion prioritizes quality, transparency, and fair wages
Patagonia and Eileen Fisher lead the slow fashion movement
The approach challenges disposable consumer culture

faq.question: Is slow fashion affordable for average consumers?
faq.answer: Individual garments cost more, but the cost-per-wear is often lower because slow fashion items last years instead of weeks. A $100 jacket worn 200 times is cheaper per wear than a $20 jacket worn 10 times. However, the upfront cost remains a real barrier for many people.

faq.question: Can the fashion industry actually become sustainable?
faq.answer: Full sustainability would require producing far less clothing overall, which conflicts with growth-driven business models. Incremental improvements like recycled fabrics and better labor practices help, but systemic change requires consumers to fundamentally buy less.
